content: Poliomyelitis, commonly referred to as polio or infantile paralysis, is an acute viral infectious disease that spreads primarily through the fecal-oral route. The term poliomyelitis originates from the Greek words polio (meaning grey), myelon (referring to the spinal cord), and the suffix -itis (indicating inflammation). Approximately 90% of polio infections are asymptomatic. However, in cases where the virus enters the bloodstream, individuals may exhibit a range of symptoms. In less than 1% of cases, the virus invades the central nervous system, preferentially infecting and destroying motor neurons. This can result in muscle weakness and acute flaccid paralysis. The type of paralysis depends on the specific nerves affected. Spinal polio, the most common form, is characterized by asymmetric paralysis, often involving the legs. Bulbar polio affects muscles innervated by cranial nerves, while bulbospinal polio is a combination of both spinal and bulbar paralysis. Poliomyelitis was first identified as a distinct condition by Jakob Heine in 1840, and its causative agent, poliovirus, was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1908. While major polio epidemics were unknown before the 20th century, the disease became one of the most feared childhood illnesses in the United States during that time. Polio epidemics paralyzed thousands, primarily young children, and caused significant morbidity and mortality throughout human history. The disease existed as an endemic pathogen for thousands of years until the 1880s, when large-scale epidemics began in Europe and later spread to the United States. By 1910, polio cases surged globally, with frequent epidemics occurring, particularly in urban areas during summer months. These outbreaks, which left many children and adults paralyzed, spurred the development of vaccines. The vaccines developed by Jonas Salk in 1952 and Albert Sabin in 1962 significantly reduced the annual number of polio cases from hundreds of thousands to around a thousand. Global vaccination efforts led by the World Health Organization, UNICEF, and Rotary International aim to eradicate the disease entirely. The term poliomyelitis refers to the disease caused by any of the three serotypes of poliovirus. Two primary patterns of polio infection are recognized: a minor illness that does not involve the central nervous system (CNS), known as abortive poliomyelitis, and a major illness involving the CNS, which can be either paralytic or non-paralytic. Poliovirus is transmitted via the fecal-oral or oral route. Acute infection typically involves the oropharynx, gastrointestinal tract, and occasionally the CNS. The virus replicates within gastrointestinal cells for about a week before penetrating the intestinal lining. Once in the bloodstream, the virus causes viremia and disseminates throughout the body. In rare cases, major viremia progresses, allowing the virus to invade the CNS and trigger a localized inflammatory response. Polio is a highly infectious disease caused by poliovirus, which invades the nervous system. Polioviruses are small, non-enveloped viruses with capsids enclosing a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome approximately 7,500 nucleotides long. The primary mode of transmission is person-to-person spread via the fecal-oral route, although oral-oral transmission may account for some cases. Due to global eradication efforts, the number of countries where travelers are at risk for polio has dramatically decreased. The last documented case of wild poliovirus-associated paralysis in a U.S. resident traveling abroad occurred in 1986 in a vaccinated adult who had been in South and Southeast Asia. In 2005, an unvaccinated U.S. adult traveling abroad contracted vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis after contact with an infant recently vaccinated with the oral polio vaccine. Poliovirus is highly contagious, with seroconversion rates among susceptible household contacts of children approaching 100% and greater than 90% among susceptible adult household contacts. Infected individuals are most contagious from 7 to 10 days before and after symptom onset, but poliovirus can be present in stool for 3 to 6 weeks. Many cases of poliomyelitis result in only temporary paralysis. However, 25% to 40% of individuals who contracted paralytic poliomyelitis in childhood may experience new muscle pain, worsening weakness, or develop new weakness or paralysis after 30 to 40 years. This condition is known as post-polio syndrome. Patients with abortive polio infections recover completely. In cases involving aseptic meningitis, symptoms typically persist for 2 to 10 days, followed by complete recovery. The clinical manifestations of poliovirus infection range from asymptomatic (the majority of infections) to symptomatic, including acute flaccid paralysis of a single limb, quadriplegia, respiratory failure, and, in rare cases, death. Laboratory diagnosis of poliomyelitis is typically made by isolating poliovirus from stool or pharyngeal samples. Neutralizing antibodies to poliovirus can also be diagnostic and are generally detectable in the blood early in the course of infection. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), obtained via lumbar puncture, may reveal an increased number of white blood cells (primarily lymphocytes) and mildly elevated protein levels. Detection of the virus in CSF is diagnostic of paralytic polio but is rarely observed. Treatment for polio is limited to symptom management, ranging from pain and fever relief to intubation and mechanical ventilation for patients with respiratory insufficiency. Two polio vaccines are used worldwide to combat the disease. Both vaccines induce immunity to polio, effectively blocking person-to-person transmission of wild poliovirus. This not only protects individual vaccine recipients but also provides herd immunity, safeguarding the wider community.
